metadata.summary: This literature review critically appraises 4 studies and presents graded clinical recommendations for degenerative cervical myelopathy. It addresses clinical assessment and prognosis using cervical MRI, surgery for mild disease, and the choice between anterior and posterior approaches when either is suitable. It also considers how pain, frailty and health-related quality of life may inform patient counseling.

A trial of structured rehabilitation or structured clinical follow-up remains a viable nonsurgical option; the review does not establish that surgery is preferable to nonsurgical management.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgical decompression
recommended_regimens.summary: Offer cervical surgical decompression as an option. In the reviewed cohorts, the surgeon selected an anterior, posterior, or combined approach, with or without instrumented fusion. The recommendation is conditional because comparative evidence against nonsurgical management is lacking.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the reviewed prospective cohorts, surgically treated patients had significant improvements at two-year follow-up: mean mJOA score (0.87), Nurick grade ( 1.13), NDI ( 12.97), SF-36v2 Physical Component Summary (5.75), and SF-36v2 Mental Component Summary (6.93). The document describes all of these as improvements but does not clearly display a sign for the Nurick grade or NDI values. Separately cited evidence associated surgery for mild DCM with an incremental lifetime gain of 1.26 quality-adjusted life years (QALY) compared with observation.

alternative_regimens.name: Structured rehabilitation
alternative_regimens.summary: A trial of structured rehabilitation is presented as an acceptable treatment option for mild DCM.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider as a nonsurgical option; the review does not provide comparative evidence sufficient to favor surgery strongly.

alternative_regimens.name: Structured follow-up
alternative_regimens.summary: Continue organized clinical observation rather than proceeding immediately to surgery.

response_assessment.method: mJOA, Nurick grade, NDI, and SF-36v2
response_assessment.interpretation: These were follow-up measures in the reviewed surgical cohorts, not a prescribed assessment schedule.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The reviewed surgical analysis lacked a nonsurgical control group and was non-randomized, with potential selection bias. The document reports postoperative complications within 30 days of surgery in 30% of patients. mJOA severity classification does not capture quality of life.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients undergoing their first operation who require decompression of at least 2 cervical levels and for whom both ventral and dorsal surgery are clinically suitable.
decision_rules: When either surgical approach is suitable, discuss ventral and dorsal decompression as providing equivalent functional recovery, pain, and quality-of-life outcomes.
Use shared decision-making to account for the approaches’ different complication profiles.
Clinical factors and imaging findings, including enthesopathies, ossification of posterior longitudinal ligament, kyphosis, and instability, can affect approach selection.

recommended_regimens.name: Ventral surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: An acceptable approach when clinical equipoise exists. The reviewed randomized trial used anterior cervical discectomy or corpectomy and fusion with anterior plating; equivalence was established for the ventral approach as a group, not separately for its component procedures.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the reviewed randomized trial, mean change in SF-36 PCS at 1 year was 5.9 for the ventral group versus 6.2 for the dorsal group (P = .86); the lack of a significant difference persisted at 2 years. All complications occurred in 48% of the ventral group versus 24% of the dorsal group. Dysphagia occurred in 41% of the ventral group, with half of affected patients still experiencing it at 6 months. The ventral treatment arm had 4 reoperations.

recommended_regimens.name: Dorsal surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: An acceptable approach when clinical equipoise exists. In the reviewed randomized trial, surgeons selected either laminectomy and fusion using lateral mass screws or open-door laminoplasty; equivalence was established for the dorsal approach as a group, not separately for either procedure.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the reviewed randomized trial, mean change in SF-36 PCS at 1 year was 6.2 for the dorsal group versus 5.9 for the ventral group (P = .86); the lack of a significant difference persisted at 2 years. All complications occurred in 24% of the dorsal group versus 48% of the ventral group. The dorsal group had no reported dysphagia and had 4 reoperations.

response_assessment.method: SF36 PCS; secondary measures included mJOA, NDI, and EuroQol 5 Dimensions score.
response_assessment.interpretation: The reviewed randomized trial found no significant difference between ventral and dorsal groups in its primary outcome or secondary measures.
The reviewed trial reported that the absence of a significant difference between approaches persisted.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Dorsal surgery had a higher incidence of impaired wound healing/infection, systemic complications, and new radiculopathy. A non-randomized secondary analysis favored laminoplasty over dorsal and ventral fusion at 2 years for the primary outcome and reported fewer complications and less postsurgical use of physical therapy and opioid treatment; the review cautions that possible selection bias requires further validation before treating that finding as definitive. Consider neurological dysfunction, neck and arm pain, medical frailty, health-related quality of life, and cervical cord MRI findings when counseling patients.

recommendations.statement: Use diffusion-weighted imaging MR signal changes in the cervical cord to help estimate prognosis after surgery.
recommendations.context: The abstract gives this imaging recommendation, whereas the detailed recommendation emphasizes using MRI findings to counsel patients about recovery.
recommendations.rationale: The reviewed study associated cord signal abnormalities with clinical severity and postoperative recovery.

recommendations.statement: Perform surgery for patients with severe or moderate DCM.
recommendations.context: This is attributed to the 2017 AO Spine/CSRS Guidelines, rather than presented as a new recommendation of this review.

recommendations.statement: Use the relationship between cervical cord MRI findings and outcomes to counsel patients about their expected recovery after surgery.
recommendations.context: The detailed recommendation discusses T1WI hypointensity and multilevel T2WI hyperintensity as findings associated with reduced recovery potential; it describes single-level T2WI hyperintensity as only weakly correlated with clinical findings and prognosis.
recommendations.rationale: The reviewed study linked MRI signal patterns to symptom severity and surgical prognosis, although the limited frequency and only fair inter-rater agreement of T1 hypointensity constrain its utility.

conditions.name: degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM)
conditions.description: A heterogeneous group of degenerative and congenital conditions that progressively compress the cervical spinal cord. The document includes cervical spondylosis and ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament within this group.
conditions.epidemiology: The document identifies DCM as the most common form of spinal cord impairment in adults worldwide and anticipates that its incidence and prevalence will rise as the population ages.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Neurological findings vary between patients and may include motor, sensory, gait and bladder impairment, as well as neck or arm pain. Presentation is influenced by the extent and level of cord compression and by overall health. Patients with similar clinical findings may have different underlying conditions and responses to treatment.

subtypes.name: mild DCM

subtypes.name: moderate DCM

subtypes.name: severe DCM
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Defined as mJOA < 12 in the studies discussed.

subtypes.name: severe multimodal impairment
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A phenotype identified in a surgical cohort, with impairment across symptom domains and the highest neck pain, NDI and frailty levels. At 1 year after surgery, this group had the greatest mJOA improvement but the poorest quality-of-life outcomes.

subtypes.name: minimal impairment
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A phenotype with little impairment across symptom domains and the lowest neck pain score. At 1 year after surgery, this group had the highest physical and lowest mental quality-of-life scores.

subtypes.name: motor dominant
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A phenotype characterized by substantial motor and sensory dysfunction with little or no pain. Physical and mental quality of life improved modestly at 1 year after surgery.

subtypes.name: pain dominant
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A phenotype with marked neck pain but better motor and sensory function than the severe multimodal impairment group. It had the highest mental quality-of-life scores at 1 year after surgery.

document_sections.heading: Abstract
document_sections.content: Study Design: This review critically examines literature on degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) and develops clinical recommendations. Objective: It addresses selected current questions about DCM management. Methods: The authors assessed recent literature, selected 4 articles and graded recommendations as Strong or Conditional. Results: The article on pre-operative MRI signal supports a Conditional recommendation to use cervical cord diffusion-weighted imaging MR signal changes when estimating prognosis after DCM surgery. The study of mild DCM supports a Conditional recommendation that surgery is an appropriate option with favorable clinical outcomes. The randomized comparison of ventral and dorsal surgery supports a Strong recommendation that outcomes are in equipoise when either approach is suitable. The phenotype study supports a Conditional recommendation to consider pain, medical frailty and effects on health-related quality of life during counseling. Conclusions: Assessment of DCM should encompass neurological impairment, pain, health-related quality of life, medical frailty and cord changes on MR imaging. Surgery is effective and is an option for mild DCM. When both anterior and posterior surgery are suitable, their clinical benefits are similar, although their complication patterns differ.

document_sections.heading: Introduction
document_sections.content: DCM is the most common cause of spinal cord impairment among adults worldwide. It includes degenerative and congenital conditions that progressively compress the cervical cord, including cervical spondylosis and ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament. Large prospective studies have found that many patients benefit from surgery and that it is generally safe and effective. The 2017 AO Spine/CSRS Guidelines strongly recommended surgery for moderate or severe DCM, classified with the modified Japanese Orthopedic Association (mJOA) instrument. For mild DCM, the preferred course is less certain: carefully observed nonoperative care and surgery remain relatively balanced options. This review aims to characterize DCM and identify important directions for further clinical research. Clinical manifestations vary considerably with the extent of cord compression, the affected cervical levels and overall health. Similar presentations may conceal different pathology or lead to different treatment responses, complicating diagnosis, prognosis and planning. The review examines assessment of this heterogeneity, the prognostic role of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) after surgery, surgery for mild DCM, and the comparative merits of anterior and posterior operations when both are feasible. These questions align with gaps identified by RECODE DCM.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: A working group of the AO Spine Knowledge Forum Spinal Cord Injury reviewed recent DCM-management literature. It chose 4 articles, one for each of the 4 specified RECODE DCM gaps, on the basis of relevance and study quality. The authors summarized and critically assessed those articles and also drew on previously published systematic reviews. They used GRADE methodology to assign clinical recommendations a grade of Strong or Conditional.

document_sections.heading: Results
document_sections.content: The working group presents critical assessments of its 4 selected articles in the sections that follow.

document_sections.heading: Article 1
document_sections.content: The selected study examines relationships among pre-operative MRI signal intensity, clinical status and surgical outcomes in DCM.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Rationale
document_sections.content: MRI contributes to DCM diagnosis. The selected investigators asked whether cervical cord signal characteristics corresponded to disability severity and whether signal abnormalities could predict outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: The investigators analyzed 2 prospective surgical DCM cohorts comprising 419 patients. They classified cord MRI findings as no signal change, T2 hyperintensity alone, or T2 hyperintensity together with T1 hypointensity, then compared these categories with pre-operative clinical status and the 2-year post-operative mJOA outcome. Baseline disease was significantly more severe with T2 hyperintensity and more severe still when T1 hypointensity was also present. At 2-year follow-up, the group with both changes had a significantly worse Hirabayashi recovery ratio than either the unchanged-signal group or the T2-only group (r = 0.209, P < .001). T1 hypointensity had the strongest correlation with disease severity, but appeared in only one-fifth of patients and had only ‘fair’ inter-rater agreement, restricting its usefulness. This retrospective analysis used the prospective multicenter AO Spine CSM-NA (Cervical Spondylotic MyelopathyNorth America) and AO Spine CSM-I (Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy-International) surgical studies. Investigators assessed sagittal T2WI hyperintensity and sagittal T1WI hypointensity at the T2WI abnormality, measured impairment with mJOA and Nurick, and evaluated outcomes at 2 years with the Hirabayashi recovery ratio and a qualified postoperative mJOA score. Among patients (n = 419), 28.9% had no signal change, 51.8% had T2WI change only, and 19.3% had T1WI + T2WI changes; 27% of the cohort had T2WI abnormalities at multiple levels. No signal-change category correlated with fewer myelopathic features, whereas more severe findings accompanied combined T2WI + T1WI abnormalities. Baseline mJOA and Nurick results worsened stepwise across the no-change, T2WI-only and combined-change groups. Patients with myelopathic signs/symptoms had significantly more T2WI-hyperintense levels than those without them. At 2 years, patients without signal changes were most likely to reach the investigators’ optimal-outcome threshold of mJOA > 16. More T2WI-hyperintense levels or combined T1WI + T2WI changes corresponded to the lowest probability of that outcome. T2WI change alone had no significant relationship with optimal surgical outcome. By the Hirabayashi recovery ratio, combined changes and a greater number of T2WI-hyperintense levels accompanied less recovery.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation for Integrating Into Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: MRI findings inform assessment of DCM symptom severity and prognosis after surgery. T1WI hypo-intense change may matter because it accompanies more frequent myelopathic features and reduced recovery potential. Multi-level T2WI hyperintensity likewise accompanies reduced recovery potential, whereas single-level T2WI hyperintensity has only weak associations with pre-operative signs and symptoms and with post-operative prognosis. Other reported measures include fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity, magnetization transfer (MT) and intracellular volume fraction, which have been shown to assist DCM diagnosis and management, respectively. FA is a measurable DTI parameter that is lower in DCM because axonal integrity is damaged. The authors make a Conditional recommendation to use knowledge of MRI–outcome associations when counseling patients about expected recovery.

document_sections.heading: Article 2
document_sections.content: The selected study evaluates the efficacy and safety of surgery for mild DCM using prospective multicenter AO Spine North American and international data.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Rationale
document_sections.content: Treatment of mild DCM remains disputed; previous guidance recommends either surgery or a trial of structured rehabilitation. mJOA grades DCM as ‘mild’, ‘moderate’ or ‘severe’ through upper- and lower-extremity motor function, sensation and bladder control, but does not capture quality of life. Surgery decompresses the narrowed cervical canal and is described as the only evidence-based DCM treatment, although complications can occur. Decisions in mild DCM therefore require consideration of functional and quality-of-life benefits against surgical risks. SF36 is commonly used to assess quality-of-life change.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: Investigators identified One hundred ninety-three patients with mild DCM (mJOA 1517) in the prospective multicenter AO Spine CSM-NA and CSM-I studies. Mean age was 52.4 years, and 34.7% were females. All underwent cervical decompression through an anterior, posterior or combined approach, with or without instrumented fusion; the treating surgeon selected the approach. At baseline, every Short Form-36 version 2 (SF-36v2) quality-of-life domain was significantly worse than population norms and comparator conditions such as asthma and congestive heart failure. Social functioning, physical functioning and mental health were particularly affected. At two-year follow-up, operated patients had statistically significant improvements in mean mJOA (0.87), Nurick grade ( 1.13), NDI ( 12.97), SF-36v2 Physical Component Summary (5.75) and Mental Component Summary (6.93). Postoperative complications occurred in 30% within 30 days; the most frequent were progression of myelopathy (6.74%), worsening axial neck pain (6.22%) and dysphagia (5.70%). The study was a post-hoc assessment of 2 non-randomized, prospective, multicenter surgical-decompression cohorts. Its prespecified severity categories were mild (mJOA 15-17), moderate (mJOA 12-14) and severe (mJOA < 12), adopted to examine whether surgical outcomes differ by severity. Eligible adults had at least one myelopathic sign, imaging-confirmed cervical cord compression and no previous cervical spine surgery. The review judges the outcomes and methods clearly described and the statistical analyses appropriate, including a power calculation whose timing relative to study initiation was unclear. SF-36v2 comparisons used a normative Canadian population. Data at 24 months were available for 93.3% of patients, and ethics approval was obtained. Study tables comprehensively presented baseline characteristics, symptoms, outcomes, operation types and complications; outcomes included means and 95% confidence intervals at each time point. The review notes that a graph comparing quality-of-life domains with population norms would have helped interpretation. The study discussion represented the results fairly, including possible reasons that the 30-meter walking test showed no improvement, and acknowledged possible selection bias. Its reported complication rate of 30.6% appears high relative to contemporary practice; predominance of anterior surgery and its frequently mild, transient dysphagia may contribute. The review considers reporting transparent but identifies the non-randomized design, absence of a nonsurgical control, possible surgeon-related selection bias and variation in surgical technique as limitations. Classification by mJOA may add selection bias because interobserver agreement is limited: mild-versus-moderate classification differs in over 10% of patients. By GRADE reporting criteria, evidence quality is moderate.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation for Integrating Into Your Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: The reviewers describe the selected analysis of prospective data as well designed and relevant to increasingly frequent mild DCM presentations in spinal surgical clinics as primary-care awareness grows. They judge that gains in function and quality of life after surgery likely outweigh complications, on moderate-quality evidence. Separately cited evidence associates surgery for mild DCM with an incremental lifetime gain of 1.26 quality-adjusted life years (QALY) relative to observation. The authors make a Conditional recommendation that surgery be offered as an option for mild DCM. Because comparative evidence against nonsurgical management is lacking, they cannot recommend surgery strongly over that alternative. Structured follow-up remains feasible for clinically stable patients.

document_sections.heading: Article 3
document_sections.content: The selected randomized clinical trial compares ventral and dorsal spinal surgery with respect to patient-reported physical functioning in cervical spondylotic myelopathy.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Rationale
document_sections.content: Cord decompression is the principal operation for DCM. Once surgery is chosen, decisions remain about anterior (ventral) versus posterior (dorsal) access and restricting versus preserving motion. Comorbidities such as enthesopathies and imaging findings such as ossification of posterior longitudinal ligament, kyphosis or instability may influence the choice, but surgeon preference often plays a substantial role. Earlier comparative research sought to clarify whether the two routes were in equipoise; most studies were observational and lacked a prespecified sample size or sufficient statistical rigor to rule out selection bias. Randomization addresses that bias and allows stronger causal attribution. Ghogawala et al therefore conducted a multicenter randomized trial of patient-reported functional outcomes after ventral versus dorsal DCM surgery.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: Eligible patients were undergoing their first DCM operation and needed decompression of at least 2 cervical levels. Investigators reviewed MRI, CT and Dynamic X-Rays to verify suitability and clinical equipoise. One hundred and sixty-three patients were randomized to ventral (n = 63) or dorsal (n = 100) surgery. Ventral procedures involved anterior cervical discectomy or corpectomy and fusion with anterior plating. For dorsal procedures, surgeons selected laminectomy and fusion using lateral mass screws or open-door laminoplasty, permitting a secondary comparison of laminoplasty with ventral and dorsal fusion. The primary endpoint was change at 1 year in Short Form 36 Physical Component Summary (SF36 PCS); secondary measures were mJOA, NDI and EuroQol 5 Dimensions. Mean SF-36 PCS change did not differ significantly between ventral and dorsal groups at 1 year (5.9 vs 6.2 P = .86), and this finding persisted at 2 years. Secondary measures, including NDI, also showed no significant between-group differences. All complications were more frequent after ventral than dorsal surgery (48% vs 24%). Dysphagia accounted for most ventral complications (41%); half of affected patients still had it at 6 months. Each surgical arm had 4 reoperations. No dysphagia was reported after dorsal surgery, which instead had higher incidences of impaired wound healing/ infection, systemic complications and new radiculopathy. In a non-randomized secondary analysis, dorsal laminoplasty yielded a better primary outcome at 2 years than either dorsal or ventral fusion. It was also associated with significantly fewer complications and less postsurgical use of physical therapy and opioid treatment. The reviewers identify this as the first multicenter randomized ventral-versus-dorsal DCM trial. A virtual surgeon-review panel helped establish equipoise and increase enrollment, but its judgment might differ from that of an individual surgeon; applying the results to a case without equipoise would therefore be problematic. SF36 PCS is not DCM-specific, although secondary outcomes including the myelopathy-specific mJOA also showed no significant difference. All measures relied on patients’ subjective reports; objective hand-function or balance measures could have reduced reporting bias. The planned laminoplasty-versus-laminectomy-plus-fusion comparison was not randomized, and only 8 of 24 surgeons performed laminoplasty. Patient selection could thus explain its apparently better outcomes and fewer adverse events, which require further validation. The review cautions that adverse-event frequencies alone do not establish how important events are to patients. Available trial severity systems distinguished ‘major’ and ‘minor’ events, whose numbers were equivalent here. Dysphagia predominated after ventral surgery and occurred much more often than previously reported; sensitive screening may explain this. In 50% of cases, it persisted at 6 months, and whether it ultimately resolved remains unknown pending longer follow-up. Patients also prioritize reoperation and adjacent-segment-disease risks, making their comparative frequency important. Overall, the reviewers consider this a well-conducted trial with predefined outcomes, clear measures and limited crossover. They assess evidence quality as high.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation for Integrating Into Your Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: The multicenter randomized trial found no significant ventral-versus-dorsal outcome difference when patients with DCM were eligible for either route. On that basis, the authors issue a Strong recommendation that, in such patients, the approaches provide equivalent functional recovery, pain outcomes and quality of life. Shared decisions should nevertheless account for their different adverse-event profiles.

document_sections.heading: Article 4
document_sections.content: The selected machine learning-based cluster analysis identifies 4 DCM phenotypes with different clinical characteristics and long-term functional and neurological outcomes.

document_sections.heading: Clinical Rationale
document_sections.content: DCM presentations differ markedly between individuals, a variation documented in early descriptions and supported by studies of recovery trajectories. This heterogeneity has important potential consequences for prognosis and treatment. Current guidance classifies severity through mJOA, but that approach has substantial limitations. Machine learning-based clustering can combine multiple sources of data to classify clinically meaningful symptom-defined subgroups.

document_sections.heading: Study Summary
document_sections.content: The selected study sought symptom-based DCM phenotypes through machine learning. It analyzed 1047 surgical DCM patients from three large prospective multicenter studies, combining demographic, clinical and surgical information with ratings of impairment, disability and pain. It identified 4 phenotypes with different symptom patterns and recovery trajectories: “severe multimodal impairment”, “minimal impairment”, “motor dominant” and “pain dominant”. Neck pain and frailty emerged as important factors not measured by mJOA. The study discussed how phenotype-specific strategies might inform personalized management. Its retrospective pooled analysis used AO-Spine CSM-NA (Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy-North America), AO Spine CSMI (Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy-International) and CSMPROTECT (Efficacy of Riluzole in the Surgical Treatment of Cervical Spondylotic Myelopathy). Collected variables included symptom duration, frailty, surgical approach and severity. NDI measured disability, Nurick grade measured gait impairment, combined upper- and lower-extremity motor and sensory mJOA subscores measured physical disability, and NDI neck-pain scores measured somatic pain. At one year, outcomes were changes in mJOA (ΔmJOA) and physical and mental quality of life (SF-36 MCS, PCS). An unsupervised algorithm, kmeans using Euclidean distance, grouped baseline severity into 4 optimal clusters. The severe multimodal impairment phenotype had abnormalities across symptom domains and the highest neck-pain, NDI and frailty levels; despite substantial baseline disability, it had the greatest mJOA improvement after 1 year but the worst quality-of-life outcomes. Minimal impairment involved low impairment in every symptom domain and the lowest neck-pain score; at 1 year it had the best physical but lowest mental quality-of-life scores. Motor dominant impairment combined pronounced motor and sensory problems with minimal/no pain and modest gains in physical and mental quality of life 1 year after surgery. Pain dominant impairment involved high neck-pain scores with relatively better motor and sensory function than severe multimodal impairment and the highest mental quality-of-life score 1 year after surgery.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation for Integrating Into Clinical Practice
document_sections.content: The authors suggest that patient-centered baseline phenotypes may classify DCM more accurately than conventional mJOA categories and could eventually support individualized care. They make a Conditional recommendation that counseling take account of neck and arm pain, medical frailty and the effect of DCM on health-related quality of life.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: Drawing on the 4 reviewed articles, the authors describe DCM as the most common form of adult spinal cord impairment and emphasize assessment across neurological dysfunction, pain, health-related quality of life, medical frailty and cord changes on MR imaging. They regard surgery as effective and as a valid choice for mild DCM. Where anterior and posterior operations are both suitable, they offer similar clinical benefit but different complication profiles. With population aging, the authors anticipate rising DCM incidence and prevalence. The RECODE DCM group identified ten research priorities, including greater awareness, better understanding of pathobiology, regenerative and reparative approaches for cord injury, improved assessment of presentation and heterogeneity, better nonoperative approaches and more personalized management. The reviewed studies provide current insights for spine surgeons while exposing gaps requiring research. These include improved outcomes measures for heterogeneous presentations, clarification of genetic effects and advances in microstructural MRI. Greater awareness and better imaging are expected to identify more mild DCM, making its clinical course an important subject for study. Evolving surgical techniques also need prospective evaluation to establish their best individualized use.
